# Performance CI maintainability review

Reviewed October 14, 2026 with `pstack:thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`, including its type-system and benchmark-checklist guidance. Source: the frozen working tree at `C:\Users\emofo\.codex\worktrees\ci-browser-quality\Damadama Rewrite`, based on application PR 11 commit `9c8437e1e4a46965513b53f60d7fa569c0fd18ea`. The scope contains seven substantive tracked changes and four untracked additions. Exact file hashes and inspection evidence are in [the detail report](performance-quality-review-details.md).

The implementation passes the structural maintainability bar. The asset gate uses Node built-ins, explicit fixed budgets, and a direct report. Browser checks reuse the existing production-built Vue fixture, API host, ordinary JWT middleware, and ephemeral PostgreSQL database. No wrapper framework, dependency, production feature, authentication bypass, or release-workflow change is introduced. No file crosses 1,000 lines, and no concretely better large restructuring was found.

One P2 coverage finding should be resolved before publication. In `tests/Browser/performance.spec.ts:88`, the first-document layout value is sampled before the creation panel opens or the habit is saved. `page.reload()` at line 115 replaces that document and initializes a new accumulator. The final maximum at line 140 therefore excludes layout shifts between initial readiness and reload. A delayed, non-input shift during creation/save can exceed the budget while the test reports success. Sample the first-document accumulator immediately before reload, after flushing rendering callbacks, and combine that value with the reload value. This preserves the direct design and avoids adding instrumentation layers. The baseline harness already samples after save, so the change also aligns the gate with its stated evidence. Full evidence and the exact observation boundary are in the detail report.

The documented production inventory, five-run request counts, duration medians/ranges, and local-fixture limitations agree with the available evidence. The docs explicitly avoid claiming production gzip delivery, live Clerk performance, a speedup, or comparable before/after timings. The fixed byte and request limits provide headroom without deriving mutable budgets from the current build. The Check trigger covers all target branches in one workflow; dependency caches, cancellation, and three-day failure retention remain practical.

I inspected the author's red log and complete green check log: four CLI tests, twelve browser tests, and fifty-one backend tests passed. These are existing author-run results, not independently rerun suites. Per the review assignment, I started no servers, ran no suites, and changed no source files. Only the review reports were written. No credential, vault, recovery identity, or fixture-token file was read.

Remediation is one bounded step: retain the first-document CLS through save, run the affected browser check, and update the report. No maintainability refactor is required.
